How to Start Investing in the Stock Market in India: A Step-by-Step Guide

From your first rupee to your first share: the order to do things in, what you need to open an account, how to place a first order, and the costs, taxes and mistakes beginners should know about.

3 min readUpdated 20 October 2026

Step 1: Get your basics in place first

Investing in shares is for money you will not need for several years. Before you start, set up the safety net that keeps you from selling at the wrong time.

  • An emergency fund of 3 to 6 months of expenses in a savings account, sweep FD or liquid fund.
  • Health insurance, and term life insurance if anyone depends on your income.
  • No expensive debt: pay off credit card balances and personal loans first. Their interest is usually higher than what investments can reliably earn.

Step 2: Decide what the money is for

Write down each goal, when you need the money and how much. Money needed within about 3 years should not be in shares, because prices can fall sharply over short periods. Goals 5 to 10 or more years away, such as retirement or a child's education, are where equity investing makes sense.

Step 3: Open a demat and trading account

To buy shares you need a trading account (to place orders) and a demat account (to hold shares electronically), usually opened together with a SEBI-registered broker. The process is online and takes a day or two.

You needWhy
PAN cardMandatory for investing and for tax
Aadhaar linked to your mobileFor online KYC and e-signing
A bank account in your nameTo add money and receive sale proceeds
A cancelled cheque or bank statementTo verify the bank account
A signature and a selfie or video checkPart of the KYC process

Compare brokers on account opening and maintenance charges, brokerage, the DP charge on each sale, and how easy the app is to use. Check that the broker is registered on the SEBI and exchange websites. Mutual funds can also be bought directly from fund houses or through registered platforms without a demat account.

Step 4: Start simple with an index fund SIP

A low-cost index fund that tracks the NIFTY 50 or a broad index gives you a share in many large companies with one investment. A monthly SIP builds the habit and avoids the stress of timing the market. Many investors keep a core of index funds and add individual shares only after they have learned to analyse companies.

Step 5: Learn before you pick individual shares

  • Understand what a share is, how the exchanges work, and how settlement (T+1) and circuit limits work.
  • Learn to read a company's results: revenue, profit, debt and cash flow.
  • Understand valuation basics such as the P/E ratio, so you know whether you are overpaying.
  • Practise with paper trading first, using virtual money, until you can follow a plan and accept losses calmly.

Step 6: Place your first order carefully

  • Choose delivery (CNC) for long-term holding, not intraday.
  • Use a limit order to control the price you pay, especially in less liquid shares.
  • Start with a small amount and check the contract note: brokerage, STT, exchange charges, stamp duty and GST.
  • Shares reach your demat account the next trading day (T+1).

Step 7: Know the costs and taxes

ItemWhat to expect
BrokerageOften zero or low for delivery trades; varies by broker
STT and exchange chargesSmall statutory charges on every trade
DP chargeA fixed fee each time you sell shares from your demat account
Short-term capital gains (held 12 months or less)20% on listed shares and equity funds
Long-term capital gains (held more than 12 months)12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year
DividendsAdded to your income and taxed at your slab rate

Tax rates are from the rules applying since 23 July 2024; check the current rules each year. Keep your contract notes and the capital gains statement from your broker for filing your return.

Step 8: Avoid the common beginner mistakes

  • Acting on tips from social media, Telegram groups or 'guaranteed return' schemes. Only SEBI-registered advisers may give investment advice.
  • Starting with futures and options. SEBI's studies found that about 9 in 10 individual F&O traders lost money.
  • Putting everything into one or two stocks. Spread money across companies and sectors.
  • Checking prices every hour and selling in panic during falls.
  • Investing money you will need soon.

Step 9: Review once or twice a year

Check whether you are on track for each goal, whether your mix of equity and safer assets still suits you, and whether any holding no longer fits your reasons for buying it. Rebalance if one part has grown far beyond its target share. Then leave the plan alone: long-term results come mostly from time in the market and from not making big mistakes.

Common questions

How much money do I need to start?

You can start a mutual fund SIP with as little as ₹100 to ₹500 a month in many funds, and buy a single share for whatever its price is. Start small and increase as you learn.

Which is better for a beginner: shares or mutual funds?

For most beginners, a diversified index fund or mutual fund is the simpler start, because it spreads risk and needs no stock picking. Add individual shares later, with money you can afford to keep invested through ups and downs.

Is it safe to invest through an app?

Use a broker or platform registered with SEBI and the exchanges, enable two-factor login, and never share your OTP or password. Your shares are held in your own demat account with a depository, not with the app.

When is the best time to start?

As soon as your emergency fund is in place and your goal is several years away. Waiting for the 'right' market level usually means missing time in the market.
